title: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
hook: the gods fear what a giant will ask for, so the goddess of speech steps into his mouth
carry: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
tomorrow: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters

segments.voice: Yesterday, in this run of Durga and the goddesses, Saraswati began as a rushing river in the Rig Veda and became the flow of learning. What are you learning slowly, under the surface? Day one thousand seventy-eight, and the end of a week.

Three brothers have been doing fierce austerities for a very long time: Ravana, Vibhishana, and the giant Kumbhakarna. Brahma, the creator, is pleased, and is about to grant each of them a boon. The gods are worried. Ravana's request is bad enough. But Kumbhakarna is enormous and hungry, and whatever he asks for, the worlds may not survive it. So the gods go to Brahma with a quiet plea. Do something before the giant opens his mouth. This path met this scene once from Kumbhakarna's side. Today it's told from the side of the goddess who walks into it.
screen: `THREE BROTHERS, THREE BOONS.` → `THE GODS FEAR THE GIANT'S WISH.` → `DO SOMETHING BEFORE HE SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: In the Uttara Kanda of Valmiki's Ramayana, Brahma calls Saraswati to mind, and she's there beside him. He asks her to go and be the speech in the giant's mouth. And she does. She enters Kumbhakarna's speech, and when Brahma asks what he wants, out comes a wish to sleep, for years and years. Brahma grants it. Then the goddess leaves him, and Kumbhakarna, himself again, realizes what he's said, and is dismayed. Look at who Saraswati is in this scene. She doesn't fight. She doesn't argue. She doesn't need a weapon. She is speech itself, and she knows that a single wish, said out loud, can change the shape of the world. Later tellers sharpened the story into a pun: he meant to ask for Indra's throne, and the word slipped and became sleep. That pun isn't Valmiki's, but you can see why people loved it. One sound out of place, and history turns. It's a little unsettling, too. The goddess of learning, used here to trip a tongue. Some readers take it as a warning about how much power our words carry. Others see her protecting the worlds the only way speech can. And with that, the week closes. Durga, the warrior who is also a daughter coming home. Kali, fierce, and still called Ma, stopped mid-dance by stillness and love. Lakshmi, who leaves where she isn't honored, and then looks long before she chooses. Saraswati, the river underground, and the voice in a giant's mouth. One goddess is still waiting her turn: Parvati.

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: notice the word before it's spoken. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then, for a little while, watch your thoughts as if each one were about to be said out loud. Notice the ones that would hurt. Notice the ones that would help. Don't stop them. Just see that there's a small gap between the thought and the mouth, and that a lot can happen in that gap. If you pray, you can ask Saraswati to guard your speech today. If you don't, just rest in the gap. The bell holds the time.
Durga. The name over a week of goddesses, met as characters: today, Saraswati, speech itself, in a giant's mouth. Today's word.

Your line: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters. Today, before one sentence that matters, pause in the gap and choose the word. Tomorrow, Parvati, and a test in disguise. Day one thousand seventy-eight. A week, done.

howItsDone: Saraswati is invoked as the goddess of speech and learning; some Hindus offer her a short prayer before study, speaking, or performance, and the story of Kumbhakarna's boon is told in Ramayana retellings and plays.

fork.setup: you're Brahma. a giant is about to ask you for a boon, and the gods fear what he'll say. what do you do?

original.note: Sanskrit: vak, speech; Saraswati is linked with sacred speech, and here she becomes the speech in a giant's mouth.

trapdoor: what you thought: Kumbhakarna was just a lazy giant who liked to sleep.
what it means: Saraswati, speech itself, entered his words so the boon came out as sleep.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda 10; the indrāsana / nidrāsana pun belongs to later retellings, not Valmiki.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda 10 (the brothers' boons; Saraswati enters Kumbhakarna's speech)

notes: Uttara Kanda 10 paraphrased: Brahma thinks of Saraswati, she appears, he tells her to be speech in the rakshasa's mouth; Kumbhakarna asks to sleep for many years; when she leaves he regrets it. Confirm details, including that the gods' fear is voiced to Brahma before the boon.
